title: ESL Teacher CV, Interview and Demo Lesson in Vietnam
description: What schools in Vietnam check on an ESL teacher CV, how interviews run, a step-by-step demo lesson plan and the questions to ask before you accept an offer.
h1: ESL teacher CV, interview and demo lesson in Vietnam: what schools check and how to get the offer
intro: An ESL teacher CV for Vietnam should make a school's checks easy: your degree, an accredited TEFL, TESOL or CELTA with its hours, dated teaching experience, the ages you have taught and when you can start. Big chains and international schools interview overseas candidates by video; smaller centres mostly interview in person, often with a short demo lesson. Plan the demo around one narrow language aim, get the students talking more than you, and ask the hard questions about pay and the work permit before you sign.
keyPoints: Put what the work permit and the centre rules test at the top of the CV: degree, an accredited TEFL, TESOL or CELTA with its hours (most employers ask for 120 or more; the law sets no minimum; say if it had observed teaching practice) and teaching experience with exact dates.

Photos, age ranges and 'native speaker' lines are employer preferences, not law: Decree 219/2025/ND-CP sets no nationality or native-speaker condition for a work permit. Non-native speakers should list their C1-level proof.

Most centre interviews happen in person; big employers such as VUS and VAS interview overseas candidates by video. A 'recruiter' who asks for money, an app download, or your ID or bank details through an unofficial channel is running a scam.

A demo lesson is short and observed: one clear aim, a warmer, clarification, pair practice, a game that uses the target language and quick feedback. Ask in advance who will watch and whether students will be there.
Do not teach real classes, paid or 'trial', before your work permit is issued: since 10 September 2026 the worker's fine is {{vnd:15000000-25000000}} and deportation is possible.
After the offer, get in writing: gross or net, guaranteed minimum hours, who pays for each document, probation terms (at most 60 days at no less than 85% pay) and the exact work location.

sections.title: What schools in Vietnam want to see on an ESL teacher CV

blocks.text: Recruiters in Ho Chi Minh City screen fast, and much of what they screen for is paperwork they will later file for your work permit. Since 7 August 2025 [Decree 219/2025/ND-CP](https://congbaocdn.chinhphu.vn/CongBaoCP/VanBan/2025/8/45798/58141-1-20251073-1074219-2025-nd-cp.pdf) has governed work permits; teachers are filed as 'experts', which means a bachelor's degree plus at least 2 years of relevant experience, usually proved with a letter from a past employer abroad. On top of that, the education rules ask centre teachers for a suitable teaching certificate. A CV that shows these facts on page one gets read; one that buries them often does not.

blocks.caption: What to put on an ESL teacher CV for Vietnam and why each line matters (sources: Decree 219/2025, Circular 21/2018, VUS hiring pages, 2026 job ads including ILA's, a January 2026 HCMC inspection report)
rows: Degree
Degree title, university, country, year awarded
A bachelor's degree is the base of the work-permit 'expert' route; ILA's 2026 ad asks for a degree of at least 3 years
Teaching certificate
TEFL, TESOL or CELTA, provider, hours, and whether it included observed teaching practice

VUS wants a 120+ hour TEFL and prefers one with an in-class component; in January 2026 HCMC's education department flagged teachers in public-school linked programmes who held only course-completion certificates instead of the required teaching certificate
Teaching experience
Employer, country, month and year from and to, hours a week, ages and levels taught
Experience is proved with letters from employers abroad (or an earlier Vietnamese work permit), so your CV dates should match the letters you can produce
Ages and exams
Young learners, teens, adults; Cambridge Starters, Movers, Flyers, IELTS
At VUS most classes are for 6 to 16-year-olds, and parents follow progress and exam results closely
English level (non-native speakers)
IELTS or a Cambridge C1 or C2 result, or a degree in English or English teaching
Circular 21/2018 asks non-native teachers at centres for Level 5 (about C1) proof unless their degree is in the language
Availability and location
Start date, where you are now, evenings and weekends available
Centre timetables run weekday evenings and weekends; some public-school agency ads ask for proof you are already in Vietnam

blocks.text: Keep it short and scannable: one page is common for teachers with little experience, two at most for experienced ones. Lead with a two-line profile (who you teach, your certificate, when you can start), then qualifications, then experience. List classroom skills as evidence, not adjectives: 'taught 8 to 10-year-olds in classes of 15, Cambridge Movers preparation' tells a director of studies more than 'energetic and passionate'.

Be exact and truthful about dates. If you have less than 2 years' experience, ask the employer which proof they will file for your work permit and get the answer in writing before you travel. Never stretch a date or ask a former employer for a letter that is not true: an employer that files altered or forged documents is fined {{vnd:40000000-60000000}} ({{vnd:80000000-120000000}} for a company, school or centre) under Decree 283/2026, and it is your permit that is put at risk. The [requirements for a work permit](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnam-work-permit-for-english-teachers) and [which certificate schools prefer](/teach-in-vietnam/tefl-tesol-and-celta-for-vietnam) have their own guides.

sections.title: Photo, age and nationality: convention, not law

blocks.text: Vietnamese CVs commonly carry a photo, and some employers ask for one outright: the British International School's portal asks applicants for a letter, CV, photo and two educational referees ([BIS HCMC careers](https://www.nordangliaeducation.com/bis-hcmc/careers)). Use a recent, plain head-and-shoulders photo in work clothes. Date of birth and nationality are also commonly included, because recruiters screen on them, but you can leave them off if you prefer and let the passport speak later.

Job ads often state an age range or 'native English speakers'; a 2026 kindergarten ad in Ho Chi Minh City asked for native speakers aged 23 to 40 ([Tuoi Tre jobs](https://vieclam.tuoitre.vn/en/search-job/expat-teacher-kindergarten.35C74DBA.html)). These are employer preferences. The work-permit decree sets job category, degree, experience and documents as the criteria, with no native-speaker or nationality condition. VUS says it considers non-native speakers who send an intro video ([VUS teacher FAQ](https://teachenglish.vus.edu.vn/?p=979)), and the usual legal route for non-native centre teachers is a college degree or higher plus Level 5 (about C1) proof and a teaching certificate (a degree in English plus a teaching certificate, or a degree in English teaching, also qualifies) under [Circular 21/2018, Article 18(6)](https://luatvietnam.vn/giao-duc/thong-tu-21-2018-tt-bgddt-quy-che-to-chuc-hoat-dong-cua-trung-tam-ngoai-ngu-tin-hoc-166595-d1.html); the work permit still needs the bachelor's degree and experience proof described above. How hiring preferences play out in practice is covered in [hiring bias in teaching jobs](/teach-in-vietnam/discrimination-and-hiring-bias-in-teaching-jobs-in-vietnam).
An intro video

A one to two-minute video of you speaking clearly, ideally explaining a classroom routine, helps where a school cannot meet you first. Film it without real students: under the Law on Personal Data Protection, in force since 1 January 2026, publishing private information about a child needs a parent's consent, and from age 7 the child's own consent too ([Lawyers' Journal](https://lsvn.vn/cong-bo-du-lieu-ca-nhan-cua-tre-tu-07-tuoi-phai-duoc-nguoi-dai-dien-dong-y-a167752.html)).

sections.title: The cover message and which documents to send

blocks.text: Most applications go by email, a careers portal or a chat message, so the cover message is a short note, not a page-long letter. International schools are the exception: they expect a proper letter written to the job.

items: Line one: the job you are applying for and where you saw it.
Line two: your degree, your certificate with its hours, and your experience in one sentence.
Line three: the ages you have taught and one concrete result or skill that fits the ad.
Line four: where you are now, your start date and your availability for evenings and weekends.
Close with what is attached and how to reach you; keep it under about 150 words.

blocks.text: Employers commonly ask for scans of your degree and certificate with the CV. Send them only to the school's official address. Genuine VUS recruitment emails end in @vus-etsc.edu.vn and VUS says that any request for money or to download an app is a scam ([VUS fake job warning](https://teachenglish.vus.edu.vn/fake-job-warning)); VAS says it never charges recruitment, training or entrance fees and warns of fake 'online interviews' run with copied contact details ([VAS warning](https://vas.edu.vn/en/news/vietnam-australia-international-school-vas-warning-about-fraudulent-recruitment-information)). Never send your passport details, ID number or bank details to an unverified recruiter. More on [spotting teaching job scams](/teach-in-vietnam/teaching-job-scams-in-vietnam).

Schools also find teachers. On eno.vn you can create a free [teacher profile](https://teacher.eno.vn) with your subjects, the ages you teach, your qualifications, a CV and an optional intro video. Only business accounts such as schools and centres can message you, and your phone number, email and CV stay hidden until you tap 'Share my contact' in that chat. For openings, [eno.vn's teaching jobs](/jobs-vietnam-expats) link to the original postings, where you apply directly; eno.vn has not verified the employers behind them and does not handle applications; never pay to get a job.

sections.title: How English teacher interviews in Vietnam run

blocks.text: Most language-centre interviews in Vietnam happen face to face, and [International TEFL Academy](https://www.internationalteflacademy.com/teach-english-in-vietnam) says you usually need to be in the country to interview. The large chains and international schools are the exception: they interview overseas candidates by video.

blocks.caption: Interview formats by employer type, from employers' own hiring pages, 2026 job ads and teacher forums (check each ad: processes change)
rows: Big language-centre chains
Online form and documents, video interview, then observation once you start
VUS: video interview with HR of about one hour; new teachers observed in the first month at full hourly pay
Small and mid-size centres
In person in Ho Chi Minh City, often with a demo lesson
Teachers on forums report demo lessons are common, sometimes taught to staff with no students present
International and bilingual schools
Letter, CV and referees through a portal, then video or in-person interviews
VAS prefers face-to-face and uses Teams or Zoom for overseas candidates; BIS asks for two educational referees
Public-school agencies
Short interview, sometimes local candidates only
A 2026 agency ad asked for proof that the applicant was already in Vietnam

blocks.text: For a video interview, test your connection, sit in front of a plain background and dress as you would for class. In person, the same advice applies as for teaching: neat and conservative clothes, closed shoes, and arrive early. Bring printed copies of your CV and certificate and your demo plan. Have a one-minute answer ready for each question below.
Interview questions to prepare for

items: Which ages have you taught, and how do you keep a class of 7-year-olds on task?

How do you handle students who will not speak? Vietnamese students often stay quiet out of respect for the teacher, so explain how you use pair work and wait time ([classroom culture](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnamese-classroom-culture-for-english-teachers)).

How do you correct pronunciation, for example dropped ending sounds such as plural -s and past -ed ([pronunciation problems of Vietnamese learners](/teach-in-vietnam/pronunciation-problems-of-vietnamese-learners))?
How would you work with a Vietnamese teaching assistant?
Can you work weekday evenings and weekends, and how many hours a week do you want?
When can you start, and are your degree, certificate and police check ready to file?
What would you do if a parent complained about their child's progress?

blocks.text: Ask your own questions too: which course books and ages you would teach, how teachers are observed and what the observation rubric covers, and how many hours new teachers actually get in their first months.

sections.title: How to plan the demo lesson: a step-by-step template

blocks.text: The school sets the length, the level and often the topic, so the first step is to ask. Before the day, find out who will watch, the learners' age and level, how long it should run, whether real students will be in the room and whether it is paid. Then plan it like a real lesson, cut to one aim.

items.title: Choose one narrow aim
items.text: Write it as what students will be able to do: 'ask and answer What do you like doing? with -ing verbs'. One aim taught well beats three aims rushed.

items.title: Warm up and set the context
items.text: A quick, active start that leads into the topic: a picture, a mime, a mystery bag. With young learners, get everyone moving or answering together in the first minute.

items.title: Clarify meaning, form and sound
items.text: Elicit the language from the context instead of lecturing, check understanding with short concept questions and drill it chorally, then individually. Include the ending sounds Vietnamese learners commonly drop.

items.title: Controlled practice in pairs
items.text: A short pair task with one right answer, such as a question-and-answer card swap. Pairs before the whole class protects face and gets quiet students talking.

items.title: Freer practice or a game that uses the language
items.text: A survey, a guessing game or a team challenge where students can only win by using the target language. Managers will ask what the children learned, so every game must produce it.

items.title: Feedback and wrap-up
items.text: Praise publicly, correct common errors as a group rather than singling one child out, and finish by showing what students can now do.

items.title: Write a one-page plan and a backup
items.text: Aim, stages, timings, materials and two problems you expect. Print copies for the observers, and plan how you will teach it to adults playing students if no class turns up.

blocks.caption: An illustrative split for a 20-minute demo; the school sets the real length, so scale each stage to fit
rows: Warmer and context
Energy, rapport, a clear link to the topic
Clarify and drill
Eliciting, concept checks, accurate models, pronunciation
Controlled pair practice
Clear instructions, a demonstration before students start, monitoring
Freer practice or game
Students talking more than the teacher, using the target language
Feedback and close
Error correction without embarrassing anyone, a visible result

blocks.text: If the demo is for a public-school agency, plan for a big class: public schools cap classes at 35 pupils in primary and 45 in secondary, HCMC primary classes often run above that, and periods last 35 minutes at primary and 45 at secondary. Whole-class TPR, chants, team games and large visuals work better than activities that need students to move around.

sections.title: Demo lesson mistakes that cost the offer

items: **Too much teacher talk.** Long explanations and lectures read as inexperience; model, demonstrate and let students do the work.
**Games with no language outcome.** Fun alone does not pass: managers and parents judge lessons by what students can visibly say or write at the end.
**Cold-calling quiet students.** Calling on a silent student without warning or wait time causes loss of face; use pairs or choral answers first, then call on named students.
**Public correction or sarcasm.** Correct errors through whole-class feedback, and avoid idioms and jokes the class cannot follow.
**Instructions without a demonstration.** Show the task with one student or the teaching assistant before everyone starts.
**Ignoring the teaching assistant.** Brief them on the flow; do not let them run your demo in Vietnamese.
**Over-running.** Observers notice a lesson that never reaches practice. Cut a stage rather than rush the end.
**No plan to hand over and no backup.** Bring a printed plan, and be ready to teach staff if no students appear.

sections.title: After the offer: questions to ask before you sign

blocks.text: An offer is the start of the negotiation, not the end. In July to October 2026 job ads, Ho Chi Minh City centres offered {{vnd:390000-600000}} an hour, and most new-teacher offers were {{vnd:430000-560000}} ([Vietnam Teaching Jobs listings](https://vietnamteachingjobs.com/city/teaching-english-in-ho-chi-minh)). 'Up to' rates in ads are ceilings, not what you will earn, so check the [salary guide](/teach-in-vietnam/english-teacher-salary-in-vietnam) and ask these questions in writing.

items: Is pay gross or net, hourly or monthly, and how many hours are guaranteed each month?
When will you file my work permit, and will I teach any class before it is issued?
Who pays for each paperwork step, and is any cost clawed back if I leave early?
How long is probation, and what does it pay?
Is the contract 12 months or more, and what will my take-home pay be?
Where exactly will I teach, and does the permit name every site?
Will you keep any original documents or ask for a deposit?

blocks.text: What the law says on each answer (probation of at most 60 days at no less than 85% pay, no deposits or held documents, final pay within 14 working days, insurance on contracts of 12 months or more) is set out clause by clause in [what to check in a teaching contract](/teach-in-vietnam/english-teaching-contracts-in-vietnam). Your employer and the Department of Home Affairs have the final word on your permit file.

blocks.title: No paid trial week before the permit
blocks.text: Some schools ask new hires to start with a 'trial week' or real classes while the permit is pending. Probation and paid trial classes are work, and since 10 September 2026 [Decree 283/2026](https://luatvietnam.vn/lao-dong/nghi-dinh-283-2026-nd-cp-xu-phat-vi-pham-hanh-chinh-lao-dong-bao-hiem-xa-hoi-440485-d1.html) fines a foreign worker without a permit {{vnd:15000000-25000000}} and allows deportation. In an April 2026 case in Thanh Hoa, officials said that bringing in foreigners without permits to teach, substitute, do probation or observe classes is illegal ([Bao Thanh Hoa](https://baothanhhoa.vn/vi-pham-trong-su-dung-giao-vien-nuoc-ngoai-tai-co-so-mam-non-283585.htm)). A demo taught to staff during the interview is part of hiring; teaching real classes before your permit is issued is not.

Before you sign, talk to teachers who work there now and ask whether pay has been on time. You can also look the employer up in [eno.vn's directory of Saigon schools](/schools), where teachers who worked or interviewed there can vote and leave moderated reviews; most schools have few or no reviews yet, so treat it as one input. Job ads still use old district names such as District 1 or Thu Duc, while official addresses on contracts and permits have used the new ward names since July 2025.

faqs.q: Is a demo lesson paid in Vietnam?
faqs.a: Schools differ, so ask before the day. If a school wants you to teach real classes before your work permit is issued, paid or unpaid, decline until the permit is in hand: officials treat trial and probation teaching without a permit as illegal work.

faqs.q: Can I do the whole application from abroad?
faqs.a: With the big chains and international schools, yes: VUS and VAS interview overseas candidates by video. Many smaller centres interview in person only, and some public-school agencies hire only people already in Vietnam.

faqs.q: Should I put my age and nationality on my CV?
faqs.a: They are commonly included because recruiters screen on them, but neither is a legal requirement for a work permit. Leaving them off is your choice; the school will see your passport when it files the permit.

faqs.q: What should a non-native English speaker add to the CV?
faqs.a: Your strongest proof of English, such as an IELTS or Cambridge C1 or C2 result, or a degree in English or English teaching. Centre rules ask non-native teachers for Level 5, about C1, proof plus a teaching certificate; with a degree in English you need only the certificate, and with a degree in English teaching you need neither.

International schools usually ask for referees, and BIS HCMC asks for two educational ones. For any school, the letters that matter most are experience letters from past employers stating your dates and role, because they are what the work permit file relies on.
